question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{y+z}{x},$ traversed along the line segment from $(-4,0,5)$ to $(-2,1,4)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-4,0,5)$ to $(-2,1,4).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(5)\,k$ and $b=(-2)\,i+(1)\,j+(4)\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\   & =((-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(5)\,k)+t[((-2)\,i+(1)\,j+(4)\,k)-((-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(5)\,k)] \\   & =((-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(5)\,k)+t((2)\,i+(1)\,j+(-1)\,k) \\   & =(2 t - 4)\,i+(t)\,j+(5 - t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2 t - 4,$ $y=t,$ and $z=5 - t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\   & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t - 4)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5 - t)k \\   & =(2)\,i+(1)\,j+(-1)\,k \\  ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{6} \\   & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\frac{y+z}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(t)+(5 - t)}{2 t - 4} \\   & =\frac{5}{2 t - 4} \\   & =\frac{5}{2 \left(t - 2\right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\   & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{5}{2 \left(t - 2\right)})\cdot \sqrt{6}\cdot \text{d}t \\   & =\frac{5 \sqrt{6}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{t - 2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z},$ traversed along the line segment from $(-2,4,-1)$ to $(-1,3,-2)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-2,4,-1)$ to $(-1,3,-2).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(-2)\,i+(4)\,j+(-1)\,k$ and $b=(-1)\,i+(3)\,j+(-2)\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\   & =((-2)\,i+(4)\,j+(-1)\,k)+t[((-1)\,i+(3)\,j+(-2)\,k)-((-2)\,i+(4)\,j+(-1)\,k)] \\   & =((-2)\,i+(4)\,j+(-1)\,k)+t((1)\,i+(-1)\,j+(-1)\,k) \\   & =(t - 2)\,i+(4 - t)\,j+(- t - 1)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=t - 2,$ $y=4 - t,$ and $z=- t - 1$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\   & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t - 2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4 - t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t - 1)k \\   & =(1)\,i+(-1)\,j+(-1)\,k \\  ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{2(t - 2)+(4 - t)-(- t - 1)} \\   & =\sqrt{2 t + 1}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\   & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{2 t + 1})\cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}t \\   & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{2 t + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(-4,0,0)$ to $(-1,-1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-4,0,0)$ to $(-1,-1,2).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(0)\,k$ and $b=(-1)\,i+(-1)\,j+(2)\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\   & =((-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(0)\,k)+t[((-1)\,i+(-1)\,j+(2)\,k)-((-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(0)\,k)] \\   & =((-4)\,i+(0)\,j+(0)\,k)+t((3)\,i+(-1)\,j+(2)\,k) \\   & =(3 t - 4)\,i+(- t)\,j+(2 t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3 t - 4,$ $y=- t,$ and $z=2 t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\   & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 t - 4)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t)k \\   & =(3)\,i+(-1)\,j+(2)\,k \\  ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(2)^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{14} \\   & =\sqrt{14}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}((3 t - 4)+(2 t))) \\   & =\cos{\left(\pi \left(\frac{5 t}{4} - 1\right) \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\   & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\cos{\left(\pi \left(\frac{5 t}{4} - 1\right) \right)})\cdot \sqrt{14}\cdot \text{d}t \\   & =\sqrt{14}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\cos{\left(\pi \left(\frac{5 t}{4} - 1\right) \right)})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\frac{5 \pi t}{4} - \pi$, $\text{d}u=(\frac{5 \pi}{4})\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{14}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\cos{\left(\pi \left(\frac{5 t}{4} - 1\right) \right)})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4 \sqrt{14}}{5 \pi}{\int }_{- \pi}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\   & =\frac{4 \sqrt{14}}{5 \pi}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\,{|}_{- \pi}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\   & =\frac{4 \sqrt{14}}{5 \pi}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi}{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(- \pi)) \\   & =\frac{4 \sqrt{14}}{5 \pi}((\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0)) \\   & =\frac{4 \sqrt{7}}{5 \pi}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(2)\,i+(0)\,j+(1)\,k$ and $b=(1)\,i+(-2)\,j+(4)\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\   & =((2)\,i+(0)\,j+(1)\,k)+t[((1)\,i+(-2)\,j+(4)\,k)-((2)\,i+(0)\,j+(1)\,k)] \\   & =((2)\,i+(0)\,j+(1)\,k)+t((-1)\,i+(-2)\,j+(3)\,k) \\   & =(2 - t)\,i+(- 2 t)\,j+(3 t + 1)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2 - t,$ $y=- 2 t,$ and $z=3 t + 1$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\   & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 - t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 t + 1)k \\   & =(-1)\,i+(-2)\,j+(3)\,k \\  ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(3)^{2}} \\   & =\sqrt{14}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\sin (\frac{πy}{4})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sin(\frac{\pi}{4}(- 2 t)) \\   & =- \sin{\left(\frac{\pi t}{2} \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sin (\frac{πy}{4})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\   & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(- \sin{\left(\frac{\pi t}{2} \right)})\cdot \sqrt{14}\cdot \text{d}t \\   & =\sqrt{14}{\int }_{0}^{1}(- \sin{\left(\frac{\pi t}{2} \right)})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=- \frac{\pi t}{2}$, $\text{d}u=(- \frac{\pi}{2})\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{14}{\int }_{0}^{1}(- \sin{\left(\frac{\pi t}{2} \right)})\,\text{d}t & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{14}}{\pi}{\int }_{0}^{- \frac{\pi}{2}}\sin u\,\text{d}u \\   & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{14}}{\pi}(-\cos u)\,{|}_{0}^{- \frac{\pi}{2}} \\   & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{14}}{\pi}(-\cos(- \frac{\pi}{2})-(-\cos(0))) \\   & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{14}}{\pi}((0)-(-1)) \\   & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{14}}{\pi}\end{aligned}
$$
